mov.prehistoric.what: Paintings, engravings and hand stencils made on cave walls and rock shelters by hunter-gatherers, from at least 45,000 years ago in Sulawesi and from about 36,000 years ago in the caves of France and Spain, among them Chauvet, Lascaux and Altamira. Animals dominate, drawn in charcoal, ochre and manganese by lamplight, often using the bulges of the rock to give them volume.
mov.prehistoric.why: It is the earliest surviving evidence of image-making and symbolic thought. Shading, overlapping and implied movement already appear at Chauvet, so skill was present from the start rather than the end of a slow evolution.
mov.prehistoric.look: Animals in profile with horns and hooves twisted toward the viewer, outlines that follow the rock’s contours, hand stencils blown in pigment, and images superimposed over millennia.
mov.egypt.what: The art of the Nile Valley from the unification of Egypt around 3100 BCE to the Roman conquest in 30 BCE, made for tombs and temples rather than for display. Its purpose was to make the king, the gods and the dead present for eternity, so a strict canon of proportion held for almost three thousand years.
mov.egypt.why: It set the first lasting canon of the human figure and a monumental stone sculpture that Archaic Greek sculptors adopted. Akhenaten’s short-lived Amarna style, around 1350 BCE, shows that the canon was a choice, not a limit.
mov.egypt.look: Composite views with head and legs in profile but eye and shoulders frontal, hierarchic scale, grid-based proportions, hard stones such as granite and diorite, and hieroglyphs naming the owner.
mov.greekroman.what: The art of the Greek city-states from the Geometric period around 800 BCE to the Hellenistic kingdoms, and of Rome, which absorbed, copied and adapted it until late antiquity. Its core idea was the idealised human body in proportion and movement, framed by an architecture of columns and orders.
mov.greekroman.why: Greek sculptors moved from the rigid kouros to the relaxed contrapposto of the Classical period in about a century, and Rome turned that legacy into an imperial language of portraiture, relief and copies. Every later classical revival, from the Renaissance to Neoclassicism, starts here.
mov.greekroman.look: Marble or bronze figures in contrapposto, drapery that reveals the body, black- or red-figure painted vases, and Roman portrait busts with unflattering detail; check marbles for later restoration and recutting.
mov.byzantine.place: Constantinople, the Balkans, Crete and Russia
mov.byzantine.what: The Christian art of the Eastern Roman Empire from the founding of Constantinople in 330 to its fall in 1453, continued in Crete, the Balkans and Russia, where Andrei Rublev and Dionisy shaped the Moscow school. Its core idea is the icon: a consecrated image through which the holy person is present and venerated, not merely depicted.
mov.byzantine.why: Iconoclasm (726–843) forced a theology of images that fixed types and compositions for a thousand years. Rublev’s lighter, rhythmic version of the Byzantine model became the measure of Russian art, and the cleaning of old icons in the early 1900s made them a source for the Russian avant-garde.
mov.byzantine.look: Egg tempera on gessoed wooden panels with gold grounds, inverse perspective, elongated figures, fixed types such as the Hodegetria and the Pantokrator, and inscriptions; check for later overpainting and metal covers (oklads).
mov.gothic.what: Painting on gold-ground wooden panels for altarpieces and private devotion, from Cimabue and Duccio in Tuscany in the later 13th century to the courtly International Gothic of around 1400 in Paris, Prague, Milan and Burgundy. Its core idea moved from the Byzantine icon toward narrative, emotion and, at court, refined luxury.
mov.gothic.why: Giotto and Duccio gave figures weight, space and feeling and prepared the Renaissance. International Gothic created a shared court style of elegant line, rich colour and closely observed detail that fed directly into early Netherlandish painting.
mov.gothic.look: Egg tempera on poplar or oak panel, tooled and punched gold leaf, ultramarine and vermilion, swaying figures in sinuous drapery, and pinnacled frames; original frames and unrestored gold add value.
mov.earlyren.what: The art of Florence and the courts of central and northern Italy from about 1400 to 1490, when architects, sculptors and painters revived classical forms and studied nature and anatomy. Its core idea was a rational, measurable world: linear perspective, solid bodies in real space and the dignity of the individual.
mov.earlyren.why: Brunelleschi’s perspective, Masaccio’s weighty figures and Donatello’s sculpture made pictures read as windows onto real space. Medici and church patronage turned artists into celebrated intellectuals and set the pattern for the High Renaissance.
mov.earlyren.look: Tempera and, from the 1470s, oil on panel, vanishing-point perspective, classical architecture, light from a single source, profile and three-quarter portraits, and gold used sparingly.
mov.northernren.what: Painting in Flanders, the Netherlands and the German lands from Jan van Eyck in the 1430s to Pieter Bruegel the Elder in the 1560s, with Dürer, Cranach and Holbein in Germany. Its core idea was the faithful rendering of the visible world, down to reflections and textures, first for devotion and then for portraiture, landscape and the open market.
mov.northernren.why: Flemish mastery of oil glazes changed European painting and was taken up in Italy by Antonello da Messina and the Venetians. Bruges and Antwerp created the first open art market, where panels were sold ready-made at fairs and in dedicated sales halls.
mov.northernren.look: Oil on oak panel built up in translucent glazes, minute detail of fabrics, metals and distant landscapes, symbolic objects in domestic interiors, and panels that can be dated by dendrochronology.
mov.highren.what: The short classic phase of Italian art from about 1490 to the Sack of Rome in 1527, led by Leonardo, Michelangelo and Raphael in Florence and Rome and by Giorgione and Titian in Venice. Its core idea was ideal harmony: nature perfected through geometry, anatomy and classical models.
mov.highren.why: It fixed the ‘grand manner’ that European academies taught for four centuries. Venice added colour and oil on canvas, which became the standard medium of European painting.
mov.highren.look: Pyramidal compositions, soft sfumato modelling, monumental idealised figures, unified light and, in Venice, oil on canvas with rich glazed colour.
mov.mannerism.what: The style that followed the High Renaissance in Florence, Rome, Parma and the French court at Fontainebleau from about 1520 to 1600. Its core idea was artifice over nature: elongated bodies, twisting poses, acid colour and ambiguous space, prized as proof of maniera, or stylish virtuosity.
mov.mannerism.why: It broke the High Renaissance balance and made the artist’s invention, rather than nature, the measure of quality. Through Fontainebleau and engravings it spread a courtly international style, and its tensions fed El Greco and the early Baroque.
mov.mannerism.look: Serpentine figures (figura serpentinata), elongated necks and hands, crowded or tilted space, cold enamel-like colour, and polished, aloof portraits.
mov.baroque.what: The dominant style of Catholic Europe from about 1600 to 1700, born in Rome with Caravaggio and the Carracci and carried to Antwerp by Rubens and van Dyck and to Madrid and Seville by Velázquez, Zurbarán and Murillo. Its core idea was persuasion: dramatic light, movement and direct emotional appeal in the service of the Counter-Reformation Church and absolutist courts.
mov.baroque.why: Caravaggio’s naturalism and deep shadow spread across Europe within a generation, and Rubens ran a studio on an industrial scale. In Rome, Bernini fused painting, sculpture and architecture into total environments.
mov.baroque.look: Strong chiaroscuro and raking light, diagonal compositions, life-size figures pressed to the picture plane, fluid brushwork in Rubens, and in Spain dark grounds with sober realism.
mov.dutchgolden.what: Painting in the Protestant Dutch Republic from about 1600 to 1680, when a prosperous trading society bought pictures on an open market rather than through church or court commissions. Its core idea was the observed world, in portraits, landscapes, still lifes, interiors and genre scenes painted with great finesse and often with a moral undertone.
mov.dutchgolden.why: It created the modern art market of dealers, specialist genres and middle-class buyers, with millions of paintings produced. Rembrandt, Hals and Vermeer made everyday subjects and psychological portraiture into high art.
mov.dutchgolden.look: Oil on oak panel or canvas, specialist genres, tonal landscapes with low horizons, symbolic still lifes, cool daylight interiors, and in Rembrandt thick impasto and deep shadow; signatures and dates matter.
mov.rococo.what: A light, decorative style that began in Paris after the death of Louis XIV in 1715 and spread to Venice, southern Germany and Central Europe until about 1775. Its core idea was pleasure and intimacy: playful ornament, pale colour and scenes of love, leisure and fantasy for private salons.
mov.rococo.why: It moved patronage from the royal court to aristocratic and financier town houses and created new genres such as Watteau’s fête galante. In Venice, Tiepolo carried it onto vast ceilings, and the view painters sold the city to Grand Tour travellers.
mov.rococo.look: Asymmetric rocaille ornament, S- and C-curves, pastel pinks and blues, feathery brushwork, pastel portraits, and in Venice luminous skies and invented capriccio views.
mov.neoclassicism.what: A return to the forms and moral seriousness of Greek and Roman art that took shape in Rome in the 1750s and 1760s, prompted by the excavations at Herculaneum and Pompeii and the writings of Johann Joachim Winckelmann, and dominated Europe until about 1830. Its core idea was ‘noble simplicity and quiet grandeur’: clear outline, still composition and civic virtue, set against Rococo frivolity.
mov.neoclassicism.why: It became the visual language of the Enlightenment, the French Revolution and Napoleon’s empire, from David’s Oath of the Horatii to imperial portraiture. It also shaped academies, public museums and civic architecture from St Petersburg to Washington.
mov.neoclassicism.look: Crisp contours, frieze-like compositions, a smooth enamel finish with hidden brushwork, antique dress and settings, and white marble sculpture with idealised features.
mov.romanticism.what: A European movement of about 1790 to 1850 that put feeling, imagination and the individual above reason and rules, in reaction to the Enlightenment and industrial change. Its painters sought the sublime in nature, history, the exotic and the irrational, from Turner and Constable in England and Friedrich in Germany to Géricault and Delacroix in France and Goya in Spain.
mov.romanticism.why: It made landscape a vehicle for spiritual and political meaning and gave colour and brushwork expressive independence. Turner’s late light and Delacroix’s colour lead directly to Impressionism.
mov.romanticism.look: Dramatic skies and seas, small figures dwarfed by nature, loose visible brushwork, saturated colour, ruins and moonlight, and contemporary or exotic subjects charged with emotion.
mov.realism.place: France (Paris and the Forest of Fontainebleau)
mov.realism.what: A French movement of about 1830 to 1880 in which the Barbizon painters took their easels into the Forest of Fontainebleau, while Courbet, Millet and Daumier painted peasants, workers and ordinary life on the scale once reserved for history painting. Its core idea was truth to the contemporary world, without idealisation.
mov.realism.why: Courbet’s Burial at Ornans and his independent Pavilion of Realism of 1855 challenged the Salon’s hierarchy of genres and cast the artist as an independent, even political, figure. Barbizon open-air study prepared Impressionism, and Realism spread to Germany, Russia and America.
mov.realism.look: Earthy palettes, thick palette-knife paint in Courbet, unidealised working figures, plein-air oil sketches of forest and field, and large canvases of everyday scenes.
mov.peredvizhniki.what: The Association of Travelling Art Exhibitions was founded in 1870 by Ivan Kramskoi, Grigory Myasoyedov and others, several of whom had walked out of the St Petersburg Academy in the 1863 ‘Revolt of the Fourteen’, and it sent its shows around the Russian Empire until 1923. Its core idea was art as social conscience: realist scenes of Russian life, history and landscape for a wide public, free of Academy control.
mov.peredvizhniki.why: It created a national school with its own market, backed by Pavel Tretyakov, who bought its work for the gallery he gave to Moscow in 1892. Its realism later became the official model for Soviet Socialist Realism.
mov.peredvizhniki.look: Narrative realism with psychologically sharp faces, muted earth palettes, vast Russian landscapes and seasons, and history or village scenes with a moral or political charge.
mov.prerapha.what: A brotherhood founded in London in 1848 by Dante Gabriel Rossetti, John Everett Millais and William Holman Hunt, who rejected the Royal Academy’s conventions, derived from Raphael, in favour of the bright colour and close detail of early Italian and Northern art. Its core idea was truth to nature joined to moral, literary and medieval subjects; a second phase led by Rossetti, Burne-Jones and Morris turned to a dreamy Aestheticism.
mov.prerapha.why: It was Britain’s first avant-garde, defended by John Ruskin, and its later phase fed Symbolism and the Arts and Crafts movement. Painting over a white ground gave its pictures a jewel-like brilliance new to English art.
mov.prerapha.look: Brilliant colour over a white ground, botanical detail painted from nature, shallow space, medieval and Arthurian subjects, and in late Rossetti long-necked women with heavy hair and sensual features.
mov.ukiyoe.what: ‘Pictures of the floating world’: woodblock prints and paintings made in Edo (now Tokyo) from the late 17th century to about 1900, showing courtesans, kabuki actors, the pleasure quarters and, later, landscapes. It was a commercial art for an urban merchant public, produced by a team of publisher, designer, carver and printer.
mov.ukiyoe.why: Full-colour ‘brocade prints’ from 1765 and the landscape series of Hokusai and Hiroshige in the 1830s made it a mass medium. After Japan opened to the West in the 1850s, the prints reached Paris and shaped Japonisme, Impressionism and Post-Impressionism.
mov.ukiyoe.look: Flat areas of colour, bold outlines, asymmetric and cropped compositions, imported Prussian blue from the late 1820s, and publisher’s and censor’s seals; value turns on an early impression, fresh colour and condition.
mov.chineseink.what: Painting in ink and light colour on silk and paper in which, from the Song dynasty (960–1279), scholar-officials turned brushwork into self-expression and set it against the polished art of court professionals. Carried through the Yuan masters, the Ming Wu School and the Qing Orthodox and Individualist painters to 1912, its core idea was that a painting reveals the character of its maker.
mov.chineseink.why: It made calligraphic brushwork, poetry and painting a single art, so inscriptions, seals and colophons added by later owners became part of the work. The canon of styles it set still frames how Chinese collectors judge quality and price.
mov.chineseink.look: Ink monochrome or light colour on paper or silk in handscroll, hanging-scroll or album form, texture strokes (cun) in rocks and mountains, inscribed poems, and the seals of artist and later owners that record provenance.
mov.academic.place: Paris, London, Munich and St Petersburg
mov.academic.what: The art taught by the academies and shown at the Paris Salon, the Royal Academy in London and their counterparts in Munich and St Petersburg, at its height from about 1830 to 1900. Its core idea was mastery of drawing, anatomy and finish in the service of history, mythology, Orientalist and genre subjects, ranked by a strict hierarchy of genres.
mov.academic.why: The Salon was the main route to fame, state purchases and private buyers, and its medals created the first international art stars. Its rejection of Manet and the future Impressionists, most visibly at the 1863 Salon des Refusés, made it the foil against which modern art defined itself.
mov.academic.look: Invisible brushwork and porcelain-smooth flesh, precise drawing, archaeological detail of costume and setting, large and highly finished canvases, and idealised nudes in mythological guise.
mov.impressionism.place: Paris and the Seine valley, France
mov.impressionism.what: A group of Paris-based painters, among them Monet, Renoir, Degas, Pissarro, Sisley, Morisot and Cassatt, who staged eight independent exhibitions between 1874 and 1886 outside the official Salon. Their core idea was to record modern life and the passing effects of light and atmosphere, painting quickly, often outdoors, in broken touches of unmixed colour.
mov.impressionism.why: They broke the Salon’s monopoly by mounting their own shows and selling through dealers such as Paul Durand-Ruel, creating the dealer–critic system of modern art. Their handling and colour opened the way for every later modern movement.
mov.impressionism.look: Visible broken brushstrokes, light palettes with coloured rather than black shadows, outdoor light and weather, cropped compositions influenced by photography and Japanese prints, and series of one motif at different times of day.
mov.postimpressionism.what: A label coined by Roger Fry in 1910 for the painters who built on Impressionism and moved beyond it between about 1886 and 1905, above all Cézanne, Seurat, Van Gogh and Gauguin. Each sought the structure or meaning that Impressionism lacked, through geometry, optical colour theory, expressive brushwork or symbolic flat colour.
mov.postimpressionism.why: Cézanne’s construction led to Cubism, Seurat’s divisionism to Fauvist colour, Van Gogh to Expressionism and Gauguin to Symbolism and primitivism. Together they mark the starting point of modern painting.
mov.postimpressionism.look: Constructive parallel strokes and shifting viewpoints in Cézanne, dots of pure colour in Seurat, thick rhythmic impasto in Van Gogh, and flat areas of non-naturalistic colour with dark outlines in Gauguin.
mov.symbolism.what: A literary and artistic movement named in Jean Moréas’s manifesto of 1886, which spread from Paris and Brussels across Europe until about 1910. Its core idea was to suggest ideas, dreams and inner states through myth, symbol and mood, rejecting both academic narrative and Impressionist observation.
mov.symbolism.why: It gave art a language for the unconscious, desire and death, linking Moreau, Redon and Puvis de Chavannes with Gauguin, Khnopff, Klimt and Munch. It fed Art Nouveau, Expressionism and Surrealism.
mov.symbolism.look: Dreamlike or mythic subjects, femmes fatales, isolated enigmatic figures, decorative line and flattened space, charcoal ‘noirs’ and pastels in Redon, and jewel-like oils in Moreau.
mov.artsandcrafts.n: Arts and Crafts and Art Nouveau
mov.artsandcrafts.place: Britain, Belgium, France and the United States
mov.artsandcrafts.what: Two linked design movements: Arts and Crafts, led in Britain from the 1860s by William Morris, which revived handcraft and honest materials against industrial production, and Art Nouveau, which from the early 1890s in Brussels, Paris, Nancy and Glasgow sought a new style based on organic line. Their shared core idea was to unite the fine and applied arts and bring beauty into everyday objects and buildings.
mov.artsandcrafts.why: They raised furniture, glass, textiles, posters and jewellery to the status of art and made the designer a modern figure, from Horta and Guimard to Mackintosh and Tiffany. Their ideas fed the Vienna Secession, the Bauhaus and modern design.
mov.artsandcrafts.look: Whiplash curves and plant forms, iridescent or cameo glass, hand-worked oak with visible joinery, stylised natural motifs, and makers’ marks or signatures that decide value.
mov.viennasecession.what: The Vienna Secession was founded in 1897 by Gustav Klimt, Koloman Moser, Josef Hoffmann, Joseph Maria Olbrich and others who broke with the conservative Künstlerhaus, part of the German-speaking Jugendstil that also flourished in Munich and Darmstadt. Its core idea, inscribed over the door of Olbrich’s Secession building, was ‘To every age its art, to art its freedom’, pursued through a total work of art uniting painting, architecture and design.
mov.viennasecession.why: It made Vienna a capital of modernism and, through the Wiener Werkstätte founded in 1903, a centre of design. Klimt’s gold-ground portraits and Schiele’s taut, anxious line opened the way to Austrian Expressionism.
mov.viennasecession.look: Gold and silver leaf, flat ornamental patterns set against naturalistic faces and hands, square formats, black-and-white geometric grids in Hoffmann and Moser design, and erotic, nervous contour in Schiele.
mov.miriskusstva.n: Mir iskusstva and the Silver Age
mov.miriskusstva.what: An association and magazine founded in St Petersburg in 1898 by Alexandre Benois, Sergei Diaghilev, Léon Bakst and Konstantin Somov, at the centre of the Russian Silver Age that ran to about 1910. Its core idea was art for art’s sake against the Wanderers’ social realism: refined nostalgia for 18th-century Versailles and Petersburg, graphic elegance and the unity of the arts in book design and theatre.
mov.miriskusstva.why: It reconnected Russian art with European Symbolism and Art Nouveau and, through Diaghilev’s exhibitions and the Ballets Russes from 1909, carried Russian design to Paris. Bakst’s and Benois’s stage and costume designs changed European fashion and theatre.
mov.miriskusstva.look: Gouache and watercolour on paper, refined line, nostalgic scenes of Versailles, masquerades and 18th-century parks, book illustration and stage designs in saturated colour, and a decorative stylisation shared with Art Nouveau.
mov.fauvism.what: Fauvism was the first avant-garde movement of the 20th century, named when the critic Louis Vauxcelles called the painters at the 1905 Salon d’Automne in Paris ‘fauves’ (wild beasts). Led by Henri Matisse and André Derain, it used pure, unmixed colour and loose brushwork to express feeling rather than describe appearance.
mov.fauvism.why: Fauvism freed colour from description and showed that a picture could be built from colour relationships alone. Its lessons passed directly to German Expressionism and, through Matisse, to later abstraction.
mov.fauvism.look: Look for flat zones of saturated, non-naturalistic colour (green shadows, red trees), patches of bare canvas and vigorous, broken brushstrokes.
mov.expressionism.n: Expressionism: Die Brücke and Der Blaue Reiter
mov.expressionism.what: German Expressionism grew from two groups: Die Brücke (The Bridge), founded in Dresden in 1905 by Ernst Ludwig Kirchner, Erich Heckel, Karl Schmidt-Rottluff and Fritz Bleyl, and Der Blaue Reiter (The Blue Rider), formed in Munich in 1911 around Wassily Kandinsky and Franz Marc. Both distorted form and colour to convey inner experience: Die Brücke through raw city scenes and nudes, Der Blaue Reiter through spiritual colour that led Kandinsky to abstraction.
mov.expressionism.why: They made emotional intensity, not optical truth, the measure of modern painting and revived the woodcut as a modern medium. Kandinsky’s move to non-objective painting around 1910–13 was a founding step of abstract art, and the Nazi campaign against ‘degenerate art’ scattered the work, which still shapes provenance and restitution today.
mov.expressionism.look: Look for jagged contours, acid or symbolic colour, mask-like faces, angular woodcut cutting and, in Blaue Reiter work, animals and landscapes dissolving into coloured planes.
mov.cubism.what: Cubism was developed in Paris from 1907 by Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque, who broke objects and figures into faceted planes seen from several viewpoints at once. It moved from an ‘analytic’ phase of muted, splintered forms (1909–12) to a ‘synthetic’ phase of flatter shapes, collage and papier collé (1912–14), while Juan Gris, Fernand Léger and the Salon Cubists spread it widely.
mov.cubism.why: Cubism abandoned single-point perspective, the basis of Western painting since the Renaissance, and treated the picture as a constructed object. Collage and construction opened the way to Futurism, Constructivism, De Stijl and most later abstraction.
mov.cubism.look: Look for faceted, overlapping planes, a narrow palette of browns, greys and ochres in early works, stencilled letters, and pasted paper or imitation wood grain in later ones.
mov.futurism.what: Futurism was launched by Filippo Tommaso Marinetti’s manifesto on the front page of Le Figaro on 20 February 1909 and taken up by the painters Umberto Boccioni, Carlo Carrà, Luigi Russolo, Giacomo Balla and Gino Severini. It glorified speed, machines, the city and war, and painted motion by fusing Cubist fragmentation with Divisionist colour; a ‘second Futurism’ continued into the 1940s.
mov.futurism.why: Futurism was the first movement run as a media campaign, with manifestos, provocations and performances that Dada and later avant-gardes copied. It shaped Russian Cubo-Futurism and British Vorticism, though its cult of war and later ties to Fascism complicate its legacy.
mov.futurism.look: Look for repeated, overlapping forms that suggest movement, ‘lines of force’, fractured light and subjects such as trains, cars, crowds and dancers.
mov.russianavantgarde.what: Kazimir Malevich launched Suprematism, an art of pure geometric forms floating on white grounds, at the ‘0.10’ exhibition in Petrograd in December 1915, where his Black Square hung across a corner like an icon. After the 1917 Revolution, Vladimir Tatlin, Alexander Rodchenko, Varvara Stepanova, Lyubov Popova and El Lissitzky developed Constructivism, rejecting easel painting for industrial materials, design, photography and propaganda in the service of the new state.
mov.russianavantgarde.why: Suprematism pushed abstraction to its limit, and Constructivism recast the artist as an engineer, shaping the Bauhaus, De Stijl, modern typography and graphic design. The Communist Party’s 1932 decree dissolving independent art groups, and the imposition of Socialist Realism, ended both.
mov.russianavantgarde.look: Look for floating rectangles, crosses and circles in flat colour on white (Suprematism), or diagonal compositions, photomontage, bold sans-serif type and red, black and white schemes (Constructivism).
mov.dada.place: Zurich, Berlin, Paris and New York
mov.dada.what: Dada began at the Cabaret Voltaire in Zurich in February 1916, founded by Hugo Ball and Emmy Hennings with Tristan Tzara, Jean (Hans) Arp, Marcel Janco and Richard Huelsenbeck, as a revolt against the First World War and the culture that produced it. It spread to Berlin, Cologne, Hanover, Paris and New York, using chance, nonsense poetry, collage, photomontage, performance and the readymade.
mov.dada.why: Dada attacked the idea of art itself and moved value from craft to the artist’s choice, most famously in Marcel Duchamp’s Fountain (1917). Its readymades, photomontage and performance underpin Surrealism, Fluxus, Pop and Conceptual art.
mov.dada.look: Look for found objects and readymades, collage and photomontage cut from mass media, chaotic typography, mechanical diagrams and deliberately absurd titles.
mov.destijl.what: De Stijl (‘The Style’) was founded in Leiden in 1917 by Theo van Doesburg with Piet Mondrian, Bart van der Leck and the architect J.J.P. Oud, and reduced art to straight lines, right angles, primary colours and black, white and grey. The Bauhaus, founded by Walter Gropius in Weimar in 1919, moved to Dessau in 1925 and Berlin in 1932 before closing under Nazi pressure in 1933, uniting art, craft and industry under teachers including Paul Klee, Wassily Kandinsky, László Moholy-Nagy and Josef Albers.
mov.destijl.why: Together they turned abstract form into a universal design language for architecture, furniture, typography and products. The Bauhaus diaspora after 1933, with Gropius and Marcel Breuer at Harvard, Mies van der Rohe in Chicago and Albers at Black Mountain College and Yale, spread modernist design across America.
mov.destijl.look: Look for asymmetric grids of black lines enclosing flat red, yellow and blue planes on white (De Stijl), and functional, machine-like forms, tubular steel and sans-serif type (Bauhaus).
mov.surrealism.place: Paris, then New York, Mexico City and beyond
mov.surrealism.what: Surrealism was launched in Paris in 1924 with André Breton’s Manifesto of Surrealism, which drew on Freud to seek a ‘superior reality’ in dreams, chance and the unconscious. Its artists either used automatic techniques to bypass conscious control (Joan Miró, André Masson, Max Ernst) or painted dream images with illusionistic precision (Salvador Dalí, René Magritte, Yves Tanguy).
mov.surrealism.why: Surrealism was the most international avant-garde between the wars, reaching Belgium, Britain, Czechoslovakia, Japan, Mexico and the Caribbean. Its exiles in wartime New York passed automatism to the Abstract Expressionists.
mov.surrealism.look: Look for incongruous juxtapositions, hyper-real dream spaces, hybrid creatures, biomorphic forms, automatic drawing and techniques such as frottage, decalcomania and collage.
mov.artdeco.what: Art Deco was the dominant decorative style of the 1920s and 1930s, named after the 1925 Exposition Internationale des Arts Décoratifs et Industriels Modernes in Paris. It combined luxury materials and craftsmanship with streamlined geometry drawn from Cubism, machines and ancient Egyptian and other non-Western sources, across architecture, furniture, jewellery, posters and painting.
mov.artdeco.why: Art Deco was the first global modern style, shaping skyscrapers, cinemas, ocean liners and whole districts from New York and Miami to Mumbai and Shanghai. In painting, Tamara de Lempicka’s glossy, Cubist-inflected portraits became its emblem.
mov.artdeco.look: Look for stepped and zigzag geometry, sunbursts, stylised streamlined figures, polished surfaces and materials such as lacquer, shagreen, ivory, chrome and exotic veneers.
mov.mexicanmuralism.n: Mexican muralism and Latin American modernism
mov.mexicanmuralism.what: After the Mexican Revolution the education minister José Vasconcelos commissioned murals for public buildings from 1921, and Diego Rivera, José Clemente Orozco and David Alfaro Siqueiros (‘los tres grandes’) painted epic histories of Mexico’s indigenous past, revolution and labour. Across Latin America, modernists such as Frida Kahlo, Rufino Tamayo, Tarsila do Amaral, Joaquín Torres-García and Wifredo Lam built distinct idioms from local traditions and the European avant-garde.
mov.mexicanmuralism.why: Muralism showed that modern art could be public, political and figurative, and it shaped the US New Deal mural programmes and young painters such as Jackson Pollock, who joined Siqueiros’s New York workshop in 1936. Latin American modernism overturned the idea that modern art flowed only outward from Paris.
mov.mexicanmuralism.look: Look for monumental, simplified figures, pre-Columbian and folk motifs, revolutionary and labour subjects and, in easel painting, intense colour, symbolic self-portraiture or Constructivist grids (Torres-García).
mov.harlemrenaissance.what: The Harlem Renaissance was a flowering of Black literature, music and visual art centred on Harlem in New York from the end of the First World War to the mid-1930s, framed by Alain Locke’s 1925 anthology The New Negro. Painters, sculptors and photographers such as Aaron Douglas, Archibald Motley, Augusta Savage, Palmer Hayden and James Van Der Zee forged a modern Black image drawing on African art, jazz and urban life.
mov.harlemrenaissance.why: It asserted Black Americans as authors and subjects of modern art at the height of segregation, and its workshops, notably Augusta Savage’s, trained the next generation, including Jacob Lawrence. Its project of self-representation runs through the Black figurative painting prominent in today’s market.
mov.harlemrenaissance.look: Look for silhouetted, geometric figures with Art Deco and African motifs and concentric bands of light (Douglas), vivid nightlife scenes (Motley), and dignified studio portraits of the ‘New Negro’.
mov.abex.what: Abstract Expressionism was the first American movement to gain international influence, developed in New York in the 1940s and 1950s by painters including Jackson Pollock, Willem de Kooning, Franz Kline, Lee Krasner and Joan Mitchell. Its ‘action painters’ made gesture and process the subject, while its colour-field wing (Mark Rothko, Barnett Newman, Clyfford Still) sought the sublime through large expanses of colour.
mov.abex.why: It moved the centre of the avant-garde from Paris to New York after the Second World War and made the huge, all-over canvas a standard modern format. Critics such as Clement Greenberg and Harold Rosenberg, and US cultural diplomacy, turned it into an emblem of post-war Western freedom.
mov.abex.look: Look for large scale, all-over compositions without a single focal point, visible drips, pours and loaded brushstrokes, and emphasis on the physical act of painting.
mov.colorfield.what: Colour Field painting grew out of Abstract Expressionism in the late 1940s, when Mark Rothko, Barnett Newman and Clyfford Still began covering huge canvases with large flat or softly brushed areas of colour. From 1952 Helen Frankenthaler’s soak-stain technique led Morris Louis, Kenneth Noland and Jules Olitski to a cooler ‘post-painterly abstraction’, named by Clement Greenberg in a 1964 exhibition in Los Angeles.
mov.colorfield.why: It replaced gesture with colour as the main carrier of feeling, and made the flat, stained canvas itself a subject. It bridges Abstract Expressionism and Minimalism and shaped abstraction worldwide.
mov.colorfield.look: Look for large fields of colour, stacked soft-edged rectangles (Rothko), vertical ‘zips’ (Newman), thinned paint stained into raw canvas, and bare canvas used as part of the image.
mov.gutai.what: The Gutai Art Association was founded in 1954 in Ashiya, near Osaka, by the painter Jirō Yoshihara, who urged members to ‘do what no one has done before’. Its artists, including Kazuo Shiraga, Atsuko Tanaka, Saburō Murakami, Shōzō Shimamoto and Sadamasa Motonaga, staged outdoor shows and performances, painting with their feet, bursting through paper screens and hurling bottles of paint.
mov.gutai.why: Gutai’s 1956 manifesto, about the encounter between body and matter, anticipated Happenings, performance and installation by several years. Through the critic Michel Tapié it linked post-war Japan with Art Informel and international abstraction; the group dissolved after Yoshihara’s death in 1972.
mov.gutai.look: Look for thick, swirling paint applied with the feet (Shiraga), torn or punctured surfaces, poured and dripped enamel, and the trace of a physical action fixed in the work.
mov.cobra.what: In post-war Paris, ‘Art Informel’ (formless art, a term promoted by the critic Michel Tapié from 1951) and ‘Tachisme’ (from tache, stain) described the gestural abstraction of Jean Fautrier, Wols, Jean Dubuffet, Hans Hartung, Pierre Soulages, Georges Mathieu and Zao Wou-Ki. CoBrA, founded in Paris in 1948 by artists from Copenhagen, Brussels and Amsterdam, including Asger Jorn, Christian Dotremont, Karel Appel, Corneille and Constant, added spontaneous, brightly coloured figuration inspired by children’s drawings, folk art and myth before disbanding in 1951.
mov.cobra.why: These movements were Europe’s answer to Abstract Expressionism, putting matter, gesture and chance at the centre of painting after the trauma of war. CoBrA’s experimental spirit fed Jorn’s Situationist International and Constant’s New Babylon.
mov.cobra.look: Look for thick, worked surfaces, calligraphic or slashing gestures, black bars and sweeps over coloured grounds (Soulages, Hartung) and, in CoBrA, raw, brightly coloured creatures and faces painted with childlike directness.
mov.pop.what: Pop Art emerged in London in the mid-1950s with the Independent Group and Richard Hamilton, and in New York around 1961–62 with Andy Warhol, Roy Lichtenstein, Claes Oldenburg, James Rosenquist and Tom Wesselmann. It took its subjects and methods from advertising, comics, packaging, celebrity and mass production, often using commercial techniques such as silkscreen.
mov.pop.why: Pop collapsed the boundary between fine art and consumer culture and made repetition, the multiple and the artist’s persona central to art. It underpins later appropriation art, Neo-Pop and Superflat.
mov.pop.look: Look for flat, bright colour, Ben-Day dots, silkscreened photographs, repetition, enlarged consumer products and celebrity faces, and a cool, impersonal finish.
mov.minimalism.what: Minimalism developed in New York in the early 1960s, when Donald Judd, Dan Flavin, Carl Andre, Robert Morris and Sol LeWitt made geometric, often serial objects from industrial materials such as steel, plywood, Plexiglas, firebricks and fluorescent tubes. Building on Frank Stella’s Black Paintings of 1959, they rejected illusion, composition and the artist’s hand in favour of what Judd called ‘specific objects’ in real space.
mov.minimalism.why: Minimalism shifted attention from the object to the viewer’s experience of space and light, opening the way to installation, Land Art and site-specific work. Its industrial fabrication and certificate-based works also changed how art is made, authenticated and sold.
mov.minimalism.look: Look for simple geometric units, repetition and seriality, factory finishes, floor- or wall-based arrangements without plinths, and light or space used as material.
mov.conceptual.what: Fluxus, organised by George Maciunas from 1962, was an international network including Yoko Ono, Nam June Paik, George Brecht, Joseph Beuys and Alison Knowles that made event scores, performances and cheap multiples. Conceptual art, defined in Sol LeWitt’s 1967 ‘Paragraphs on Conceptual Art’, held that the idea is the work, using language, instructions, photographs and documents by artists such as Joseph Kosuth, Lawrence Weiner, On Kawara, John Baldessari and Hanne Darboven.
mov.conceptual.why: Both dematerialised the art object and challenged the gallery system, making instruction, documentation and context central. Their legacy runs through installation, performance, institutional critique and the conceptualisms of Latin America, Eastern Europe and Asia.
mov.conceptual.look: Look for text, instructions, certificates, typewritten documents and photographs, boxed multiples and scores, date paintings, and works that exist primarily as an idea or action.
mov.arteprovera.what: Arte Povera (‘poor art’) was named by the critic Germano Celant for a 1967 exhibition in Genoa and gathered Italian artists including Michelangelo Pistoletto, Alighiero Boetti, Mario Merz, Jannis Kounellis, Giuseppe Penone, Pino Pascali, Luciano Fabro and Giovanni Anselmo. They used humble and organic materials such as earth, rags, wood, stone, fat, live animals and neon to set nature, memory and energy against consumer and technological culture.
mov.arteprovera.why: Arte Povera was Europe’s most influential response to Minimalism and Pop, bringing process, perishable materials and the body into sculpture and installation. It made Turin and Rome centres of the late-1960s avant-garde.
mov.arteprovera.look: Look for raw materials in tension or transformation, mirror paintings with photographic figures (Pistoletto), igloos and neon Fibonacci numbers (Merz), embroidered world maps (Boetti) and trees carved back to their growth rings (Penone).
mov.monoha.what: Mono-ha (‘School of Things’) was a loose group of artists in Tokyo from about 1968 to the mid-1970s, including Lee Ufan, Nobuo Sekine, Kishio Suga, Koji Enokura and Susumu Koshimizu. They arranged largely unaltered natural and industrial materials such as stone, wood, steel plate, glass, paper and earth to reveal relationships between objects, space and perception rather than to make images.
mov.monoha.why: Mono-ha broke with Western-style object-making in Japan and became an Asian counterpart to Arte Povera and post-Minimalism. Its starting point is usually given as Sekine’s Phase—Mother Earth (1968), an earth cylinder beside the hole it came from in Kobe’s Suma Rikyu Park.
mov.monoha.look: Look for raw stones resting on glass or steel, materials held in tension or balance, minimal intervention, and temporary arrangements that survive as remakes and photographs.
mov.dansaekhwa.what: Dansaekhwa (‘monochrome painting’) describes Korean abstraction of the 1970s by Park Seo-bo, Ha Chong-hyun, Yun Hyong-keun, Chung Sang-hwa, Lee Ufan and Kwon Young-woo, framed by shows such as ‘Five Korean Artists, Five Kinds of White’ at Tokyo Gallery in 1975. Through repetitive, labour-intensive processes, such as pencil lines drawn into wet paint, oil pushed through hemp, and layered and peeled surfaces, they made restrained fields of near-monochrome colour.
mov.dansaekhwa.why: Under the Park Chung-hee dictatorship it offered a meditative abstraction rooted in materials such as hanji paper and hemp, distinct from Western Minimalism. Its revival from 2014 put Korean modernism into international museums and salerooms.
mov.dansaekhwa.look: Look for near-monochrome surfaces in white, beige, umber or blue built up by repetition: scored pencil lines (Park), paint pushed through hemp from the back (Ha), bleeding umber bars (Yun) and grids of flaking paint (Chung).
mov.photorealism.what: Photorealism emerged in the United States in the late 1960s, when painters such as Richard Estes, Chuck Close, Robert Bechtle, Ralph Goings, Audrey Flack and Malcolm Morley began transferring photographs onto canvas with meticulous, often airbrushed precision. Named by the dealer Louis K. Meisel around 1969 and showcased at Documenta 5 in 1972, it took ordinary American motifs such as storefronts, cars, diners, suburban houses and faces.
mov.photorealism.why: Photorealism reasserted painting and figuration against Minimalism and Conceptual art while making the camera’s way of seeing its real subject. It ran parallel to Gerhard Richter’s photo-paintings and anticipated later art built from photographic and digital images.
mov.photorealism.look: Look for crisp, even focus across the whole picture, reflections in glass and chrome, grid-transferred faces at monumental scale, and a deadpan, camera-like neutrality.
mov.neoexpressionism.what: Neo-Expressionism was the return of large, figurative, emotionally charged painting around 1978–80, led in Germany by Georg Baselitz, Anselm Kiefer, A.R. Penck and Jörg Immendorff, in Italy by the Transavanguardia (Sandro Chia, Francesco Clemente, Enzo Cucchi) and in the United States by Julian Schnabel and David Salle. In downtown New York it overlapped with graffiti and the East Village scene, where Jean-Michel Basquiat moved from SAMO© street tags to canvases mixing text, anatomy, Black history and art history.
mov.neoexpressionism.why: It ended the dominance of Minimal and Conceptual art and fuelled the booming 1980s gallery market in SoHo and the East Village. Basquiat, who died in 1988 aged 27, became the decade’s defining figure and an anchor of today’s contemporary auction market.
mov.neoexpressionism.look: Look for raw, expressive brushwork at large scale, crude or crowned figures, crossed-out words and lists, collage, and references to myth, history and the street.
mov.pictures.what: The Pictures Generation takes its name from ‘Pictures’, a 1977 exhibition at Artists Space in New York organised by the critic Douglas Crimp, and describes artists such as Cindy Sherman, Richard Prince, Barbara Kruger, Sherrie Levine, Louise Lawler, Robert Longo and Jack Goldstein. Raised on television, film and advertising, they re-photographed, cropped and restaged mass-media images to expose how pictures shape identity, desire and power.
mov.pictures.why: Their appropriation challenged originality and authorship and made photography central to contemporary art. Their methods anticipate today’s image culture of remix and social media, and Prince’s re-photographed images became test cases in copyright law.
mov.pictures.look: Look for re-photographed adverts and film stills, staged self-portraits in roles, bold red, white and black text over found photographs (Kruger), and copies of famous works presented as new work (Levine).
mov.yba.what: The Young British Artists emerged from Goldsmiths College in London with ‘Freeze’, a 1988 warehouse exhibition in Docklands organised by Damien Hirst, and were promoted by the collector Charles Saatchi. Artists including Hirst, Tracey Emin, Sarah Lucas, Rachel Whiteread, Chris Ofili, Marc Quinn, Gary Hume and Jenny Saville made provocative, media-savvy work from animals in formaldehyde, unmade beds, casts and elephant dung.
mov.yba.why: The YBAs made London a global centre for contemporary art and helped create the climate for Tate Modern (2000) and Frieze Art Fair (2003). ‘Sensation’, the 1997 show of Saatchi’s collection at the Royal Academy, made them household names.
mov.yba.look: Look for provocative materials and titles, vitrines and preserved animals, spot and spin paintings, confessional text and neon (Emin), casts of negative space (Whiteread), and a frankly entrepreneurial approach to production.
mov.chinesecontemporary.what: Chinese contemporary art grew from the ’85 New Wave, when groups across China absorbed Western modernism after the Cultural Revolution, culminating in the ‘China/Avant-Garde’ exhibition at the National Art Museum in Beijing in February 1989. After Tiananmen, Political Pop (Wang Guangyi), Cynical Realism (Fang Lijun, Yue Minjun), Zhang Xiaogang’s Bloodline portraits and Zeng Fanzhi’s Mask series found Western collectors, followed by Ai Weiwei, Xu Bing, Cai Guo-Qiang and younger painters such as Liu Ye.
mov.chinesecontemporary.why: It gave the world a visual language for China’s transformation and helped make Beijing, Shanghai and Hong Kong major art-market centres. Its auction boom of the mid-2000s, led by Sotheby’s and Christie’s in Hong Kong, was one of the first speculative surges in contemporary art.
mov.chinesecontemporary.look: Look for ironic propaganda and consumer imagery (Political Pop), grinning or yawning self-caricatures, sepia family portraits linked by red lines, masked figures, and invented or deconstructed Chinese characters.
mov.indianmodern.n: Progressive Artists’ Group and Indian modernism
mov.indianmodern.what: The Progressive Artists’ Group was founded in Bombay in December 1947, months after Independence, by F.N. Souza with S.H. Raza, M.F. Husain, K.H. Ara, H.A. Gade and S.K. Bakre, and later drew in V.S. Gaitonde, Tyeb Mehta, Akbar Padamsee and Krishen Khanna. They rejected both academic realism and the nationalist Bengal School, fusing European modernism, from Expressionism and Cubism to abstraction, with Indian subjects, colour and philosophy.
mov.indianmodern.why: They defined a secular, cosmopolitan modern art for the new republic, building on pioneers such as Amrita Sher-Gil. Their work now anchors South Asian art at auction and in collections from the Kiran Nadar Museum of Art in Delhi to Tate.
mov.indianmodern.look: Look for bold distorted figures and heavy black outlines (Souza), horses and village scenes in planar colour (Husain), the bindu circle and hot geometric colour (Raza), luminous layered abstraction (Gaitonde) and split figures and diagonals (Tyeb Mehta).
mov.africanmodern.n: African modernism and contemporary African art
mov.africanmodern.place: Lagos, Zaria, Khartoum, Dakar, Johannesburg and the diaspora
mov.africanmodern.what: African modernism took shape around independence from the 1950s in centres such as the Zaria Art Society and Mbari Club in Nigeria, the Khartoum School in Sudan and the École de Dakar, alongside earlier figures such as Ben Enwonwu and Irma Stern. Artists such as Uche Okeke, Ibrahim El-Salahi, Skunder Boghossian, Gerard Sekoto and Ernest Mancoba fused local forms, scripts and myths with international modernism, and since the 1990s El Anatsui, William Kentridge, Yinka Shonibare and Njideka Akunyili Crosby have made African art central to global contemporary art.
mov.africanmodern.why: Its ‘natural synthesis’ (Uche Okeke’s term) of local and modern traditions rejected the idea that modernism was a Western export. Okwui Enwezor’s exhibitions and the growth of fairs and biennials in Lagos, Johannesburg, Dakar and Marrakech built the institutional and market infrastructure.
mov.africanmodern.look: Look for uli line drawing (Nsukka), Arabic calligraphy fused with figuration (El-Salahi), elegant elongated figures (Enwonwu), bottle-top and metal tapestries (El Anatsui), Dutch wax-print fabric (Shonibare) and layered photo-transfer interiors (Akunyili Crosby).
mov.streetart.place: New York, then London, Bristol, Paris and worldwide
mov.streetart.what: Graffiti writing grew on New York subway trains in the early 1970s, and by about 1980 artists including Jean-Michel Basquiat, Keith Haring, Lee Quiñones, Lady Pink and Futura brought it into galleries. From the 1990s ‘street art’ widened into stencils, posters, stickers and murals, led by Banksy from Bristol, Shepard Fairey, Invader and JR, and by KAWS, whose cartoon characters crossed from the street into toys and sculpture.
mov.streetart.why: It turned public space into a gallery and built careers outside the institutions through anonymity, humour and political messaging. Banksy’s stunts and Fairey’s 2008 Obama ‘Hope’ poster showed how street imagery could dominate mass media.
mov.streetart.look: Look for spray-paint and stencil techniques, wheatpaste posters, tags and lettering, satirical slogans and recurring characters, and for official authentication, such as Banksy’s Pest Control certificates.
mov.digital.what: Digital art began in the 1960s with plotter drawings by Frieder Nake, Georg Nees, Vera Molnár and A. Michael Noll, and grew through computer graphics, net art and generative software. From 2017 non-fungible tokens (NFTs) on blockchains such as Ethereum let unique or limited digital works be owned, traded and authenticated online, and a speculative boom in 2021 brought them into the major auction houses.
mov.digital.why: NFTs gave digital art a native system of ownership, provenance and resale royalties and brought crypto-wealthy collectors into the market. The 2022 crypto crash exposed the speculation, but generative and AI-driven work has kept a place in museums and salerooms.
mov.digital.look: Look for generative code and algorithmic variation, pixel and 3D-rendered imagery, on-chain metadata and provenance, editions minted on Ethereum or Tezos, and screen-based or hybrid physical-digital works.
mov.ultracontemporary.place: London, New York, Los Angeles and Hong Kong
mov.ultracontemporary.what: Ultra-contemporary is a market category rather than a style: work by artists born after about 1975, much of it figurative painting, that reached auction within a few years of being made. Between about 2018 and 2022 names such as Amoako Boafo, Jadé Fadojutimi, Flora Yukhnovich, Avery Singer, Salman Toor and Anna Weyant were bid far above estimate in London, New York and Hong Kong, often soon after their first gallery shows.
mov.ultracontemporary.why: The boom brought new, younger and Asian buyers into evening sales and made ‘flipping’, the quick resale of primary-market purchases at auction, a central concern for galleries. It also widened representation, with women and artists of African descent prominent among the leading names.
mov.ultracontemporary.look: Look for large, saturated figurative canvases, flattened interiors and portraits, often of Black subjects, Rococo-inspired abstraction (Yukhnovich) and digitally planned painting (Singer), and check the auction trail: estimates, guarantees and how often works are resold.
mov.superflat.what: Superflat was named by Takashi Murakami in a 2000 exhibition in Tokyo, which travelled to Los Angeles in 2001, to describe a flattened Japanese visual culture linking Edo-period painting and ukiyo-e to anime, manga and otaku consumerism. It sits within a wider Japanese contemporary market led by Murakami, Yoshitomo Nara, whose wide-eyed children mix punk and childhood, and Yayoi Kusama, whose polka dots, Infinity Nets and mirror rooms date back to her New York years of 1958–73.
mov.superflat.why: Superflat erased the line between fine art and commercial production, with Murakami’s Kaikai Kiki studio making paintings, merchandise and brand collaborations such as Louis Vuitton (2003–15). It gave Japanese pop culture a place in museums and made Kusama, Nara and Murakami among the most widely collected artists in Asia.
mov.superflat.look: Look for flat, saturated colour and crisp outlines, cartoon characters such as Mr DOB and smiling flowers (Murakami), defiant big-headed children (Nara), and repeated dots and nets (Kusama).
